content: St. John’s Wort, scientifically known as Hypericum perforatum, is a yellow-flowering, rhizomatous perennial herb native to Europe. It has been introduced to the Americas and grows wild in many meadows. The plant is named for its traditional flowering and harvesting on St. John’s Day, June 24. The genus name Hypericum is derived from the Greek words hyper (above) and eikon (picture), referencing its historical use to ward off evil by hanging the plant over pictures in homes during St. John’s Day. The species name perforatum refers to the small oil glands in the leaves that appear as translucent dots when held against light, giving the leaves a perforated appearance. Approximately 370 species of the genus Hypericum exist worldwide, with a native distribution in temperate and subtropical regions of North America, Europe, Asia Minor, Russia, India, and China. While Hypericum perforatum is cultivated commercially in some parts of southeastern Europe, it is considered a noxious weed in over 20 countries. In pastures, it acts as both a toxic and invasive weed, replacing useful vegetation and rendering productive land unviable. When ingested by livestock, it can cause photosensitization, central nervous system depression, spontaneous abortion, and even death. Effective herbicides for its control include 2,4-D, picloram, and glyphosate. In western North America, three beetles (Chrysolina quadrigemina, Chrysolina hyperici, and Agrilus hyperici) have been introduced as biocontrol agents. The plant can be identified by its yellow, five-petaled flowers, approximately 20 mm in diameter, which bloom from late spring to early or mid-summer. The leaves exhibit translucent dots when held up to light, giving them a perforated appearance. When the flowers or seed pods are crushed, they release a reddish-purple liquid. Botanically, St. John’s Wort is a perennial plant with extensive creeping rhizomes. Its stems are erect, branched in the upper sections, and can grow up to 1 meter in height. The leaves are narrow, oblong, stalkless, and yellow-green in color, with transparent dots throughout the tissue and occasional black dots on the lower surface. The flowers, which are bright yellow with conspicuous black dots, appear in broad cymes at the ends of the upper branches. The sepals are pointed and contain glandular dots, while the numerous stamens are united at the base into three bundles. The plant contains various chemical compounds, including flavonoids (e.g., rutin, hyperoside, quercetin), phenolic acids (e.g., chlorogenic acid), naphthodianthrones (e.g., hypericin, pseudohypericin), phloroglucinols (e.g., hyperforin), and essential oils (mainly sesquiterpenes). The naphthodianthrones hypericin and pseudohypericin, along with the phloroglucinol derivative hyperforin, are believed to be the active components responsible for its medicinal effects. Ecologically, St. John’s Wort has a complex life cycle involving both vegetative and sexual reproduction. It thrives in areas with either winteror summer-dominant rainfall patterns but is limited by environmental factors such as low temperatures, high altitudes, and insufficient rainfall. The plant can adapt its growth form and habit to promote survival under varying conditions, including defoliation by insects or grazing. In livestock, St. John’s Wort poisoning can occur at high doses, leading to symptoms such as restlessness, skin irritation, photosensitization, and central nervous system depression. Behavioral signs include pawing, head shaking, and hyperactivity, while physical signs include reddening and inflammation of non-pigmented skin areas. Severe cases may result in weight loss, reduced milk production, spontaneous abortion, or death. Early diagnosis involves observing increased respiration, heart rate, and body temperature. Photosensitization, the primary cause of clinical signs, occurs due to the activation of photodynamic compounds in the plant by light, leading to oxidative tissue damage. St. John’s Wort is also used as a herbal treatment for depression, particularly mild to moderate cases. In some countries, such as Germany, it is commonly prescribed for children and adolescents. Standardized extracts are available over the counter in various forms, including tablets, capsules, teas, and tinctures. Clinical studies have shown mixed results regarding its efficacy. While some meta-analyses suggest it is effective for mild to moderate depression with fewer side effects than conventional antidepressants, other studies, including a major NIH-funded trial, found no significant benefit in treating major depressive disorder. The pharmacological mechanism of St. John’s Wort is thought to involve the inhibition of serotonin reuptake, similar to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). The active antidepressant constituents are believed to be hyperforin and hypericin, although other compounds like flavonoids may also contribute. Hyperforin has been shown to inhibit the uptake of serotonin, dopamine, noradrenaline, GABA, and glutamate. St. John’s Wort has other medical uses, such as reducing alcohol intake, and its aerial parts can be used to make herbal tea with medicinal properties. It has also demonstrated antibacterial activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Adverse effects of St. John’s Wort are generally mild and include gastrointestinal symptoms, dizziness, fatigue, and photosensitivity. Rarely, it may cause mania in bipolar patients or interact with other medications, including oral contraceptives, reducing their effectiveness. It can also induce the cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP3A4, leading to increased metabolism and reduced efficacy of certain drugs. Additionally, it may contribute to serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic drugs. Historically, St. John’s Wort has been used for medicinal purposes since ancient Greece and by Native Americans as an abortifacient and anti-inflammatory agent. Its flowers and stems have also been used to produce red and yellow dyes.
